concept.name: Central limit theorem
concept.definition: The theorem that the sampling distribution of the sample mean (or sum) of independent observations approaches a normal distribution as the sample size grows, regardless of the shape of the original distribution - provided its variance is finite. The limiting normal has the population mean mu and standard deviation sigma/sqrt(n).
concept.intuition: Averages of many small, independent influences look bell-shaped even when the individual influences are not - which is why so many statistics can be treated as approximately normal with enough data.
concept.mechanics: Draw random samples of size n and compute their means; the distribution of those means centers on mu with spread sigma/sqrt(n) (the standard error) and becomes increasingly normal in shape as n grows. A common rule of thumb takes n >= 30 as 'large enough' for roughly symmetric populations, with more needed for skewed ones.
concept.formula: For i.i.d. X_i with mean mu and standard deviation sigma, the sample mean x_bar is approximately N(mu, sigma^2/n) for large n; equivalently z = (x_bar - mu) / (sigma/sqrt(n)) approaches the standard normal distribution.
concept.failure_modes: The CLT requires independence and finite variance: heavy-tailed return distributions with infinite variance never converge to normal, and autocorrelated data converge far more slowly than the i.i.d. rate. The approximation is also weakest in the tails - exactly where financial risk questions live - so CLT-based tail probabilities can be badly wrong even at moderate n.
concept.misconceptions: The CLT does not say the data themselves become normal, only the distribution of the mean or sum; individual returns can stay fat-tailed forever. Nor is n = 30 a law - skewed or heavy-tailed populations need much larger n, and no n suffices when the variance does not exist.
concept.example: Daily trade P&Ls are right-skewed, but the mean P&L of 100 independent trades is approximately normal with standard deviation sigma/10, enabling a z-test on the strategy's average edge.
